Overall, this game is fire and a must play in my own opinion, and I don't even like retro fighting games such as Street Fighter or Tekken that much. I'd definitely wait for it to go on sale because If you finish the game, there probably isn't much replay ability unless you start all over again. Karate Master 2: Knock Down Blow es un juego muy particular, pensado claramente para un público concreto. No intenta competir con grandes juegos de lucha ni ser accesible para todo el mundo, sino ofrecer una experiencia centrada en el karate tradicional, con un enfoque más técnico que espectacular.

El sistema de combate es su mayor atractivo. Los enfrentamientos son duros, lentos y exigentes, y premian la colocación, el timing y la lectura del rival más que la ejecución de combos. Aquí cada golpe importa, y un error se paga caro. Cuando el sistema encaja, transmite muy bien la sensación de combate físico y tenso.

El problema es que esa misma filosofía también limita el juego. El ritmo puede resultar demasiado rígido y tosco, especialmente para jugadores acostumbrados a luchadores más fluidos. Las animaciones son funcionales, pero poco refinadas, y el control requiere paciencia para no sentirse frustrante.

En cuanto a contenido, es correcto sin destacar. Hay modos suficientes para entretener durante unas horas, pero la variedad es limitada y el juego no tiene profundidad como para mantener el interés a muy largo plazo. La progresión se siente simple y los desafíos acaban repitiéndose.

Visualmente cumple, pero sin alardes, y el apartado sonoro es discreto. Todo el conjunto transmite la sensación de un proyecto modesto, hecho con una idea clara, pero sin el presupuesto ni el pulido de producciones mayores.

En resumen, Karate Master 2: Knock Down Blow es un título recomendable si buscas un juego de lucha diferente, más realista y pausado, y estás dispuesto a aceptar controles duros y un acabado sencillo. No es para todos los públicos, pero dentro de su nicho ofrece una experiencia honesta y coherente con lo que propone.

As the 20th century Karate tribute, it is a decent thing. As a game with that price tag, though... Nah, it's not. 

All those Japanese terms, from Maai and Sen Sen no Sen to Ippon! - sounds solid. The battle system is fast and fluid, with decent hitboxes and nice moves (Waza), and not only the Karate ones, but also some distinctive moves from Box and Muai Thai, for some of your opponents. In short, all those things you see in the trailer on the store page, are there, and feels good. But... that's hardly enough.

Let's say gameplay-wise, about the game which is looks like browser things from late '00s-early '10s, but rarely sells for less than 5$, even the decade after the release. First, forget about achievements - they are broken, and the dev is long gone from the game support cycle. Second, the game pace is irritating. It is not ultimately hard, but surely annoying - and I'm a fan of such games, I can mash the 'train' buttons in Punch Club all night long, as long as it provides some steady progress that makes a difference in fights, in other word, keeps my dopamine where I want it.

First, you play a lame minigame to make a quick $, just enough to pay for one or two tries to enter the basic tournament. Then you mash the buttons to beat 3 karatekas, each of them can suddenly one-punch you to the hospital. Beating the tournament provides the access to one training session. Now, trainings. You have 5 stats, and the only one that really provides (but not ultimately) is the strength. Raising it from the starting 1 to final 10 (which takes about 15-20 training sessions) makes the fights much faster and certainly improves the win rate. On the other hand, the endurance exercises still not protecting you from one-punch sudden KOs, and also, the training minigames for endurance are also the most irritating and less rewarding, out of all trainings. And some of the trainings breaking up the whole lame UI, so you basically soft-lock yourself and need to restart the game...

After you beat enough basic tournaments, you'll get the fame to challenge other karate (and not only karate) dojos, which will ultimately lead you to the best karate master in the town, and then to final Kumite tournament, with the very final boss.

Beating it all, I can say it's not worth the price, and even more, the time to grind through all the similar irritating minigames. As of summary, there were some nice points, from the basic True Karate forms, like how I remember them, trained and watched all those fighting movies in '80s and '90s, to the one or two decent minigames in training section. But overall, it's only good enough for a browser free-to-play session. Mark is 5.5/10.

ステータスの内容はゲーム中に説明がないので参考程度に。
・強さ 攻撃力が上がる。最優先で鍛えるべし！
・タフさ 防御力が上がる。タフすぎてソンはない。
・スピード 技の発生が速くなる。
・体鍛え クリティカル率アップ。一撃必殺が出やすくなるっぽい。

ただし、修行するにはトレーニングポイントが必要。
トレーニングポイントは大会で優勝するか、道場破りをして勝利すると手に入る。
俺は、最初から最後までコブラ会狩りをしてトレーニングポイントを貯めた。
またポイントを消費してカカト落とし、胴回し回転蹴りなどの[strike]全く役に立たない[/strike]新技を会得出来る。
ただし、大会に参加するにはお金が必要でフォークリフトのミニゲームで稼ぐ必要がある。
たまにバグで荷物が出て来なくて、時間切れまで何も出来ない事が結構あった･･･

赤の状態で攻撃を食らうと一本負けになる。
またランダムで「一撃必殺」が発動すると即KOとなる。
敵の種類によっては結構な頻度で一撃必殺してくるので注意！
ボクシング、ムエタイ、テコンドー、プロレスとの異種格闘大会、

This is my favorite fighting game after Hellish Quart.  I can't say it's realistic to the point of being a simulation, but it's probably one of the most realistic fighting games, and masterfully executed as an indie title.  Like any good story that blends fantasy and reality, things start low-key and relatively realistic, and become more and more fantastical and superpowered slowly and over time, as you become more invested.  The hand-drawn art style is timeless, because hand drawings will never look dated in the way that old sprites or 3d models will.  It's subtle, but the hand-drawn art style looks like sketches or cartoons from a high school student's notebook, which alludes to the adolescent fantasy aspects of the game as it gradually grows towards the fantastic and the overpowered.  As a further kind of homage to adolescence, the game makes references to martial arts popular movies and heroes from the 1970s and 1980s, as well as historical karate-related figures like Mas Oyama, allowing middle aged players today to revisit and explore their own martial arts related adolescent fantasies and perhaps reflect upon them in hindsight.

Besides for this, the karate fighting, especially at the beginning of the game before things become very fantastical, is well represented.  I've always enjoyed combative sports in real life and find the martial arts sparring gameplay to be satisfying and more or less reflecting the dynamics in martial arts sparring back in the 90s and 2000s.  If you want to kick your opponent in the leg, the best time is when he steps forward or when he puts his leg down after throwing a kick.  If you kick at the leg when the opponent is in a neutral position he may counter by kicking your head with the leg you were aiming at.  And a good push kick can interrupt an out-of-range punch or roundhouse kick that takes a longer path to its target if aimed and timed correctly.  Pretty good for a low budget indie game! What I like about this game is that someone might learn something real about karate sparring from this game, moreso than they would from some of the big name titles that are out there thes days.

So I say, you can't go wrong with this game...and you might even learn something!

[h2] GOOD [/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b] Unique Karate Adventure Concept [/b]  
Karate Master 2 stands out with its blend of fighting, RPG elements, and life simulation—you’re not just battling, you’re grinding for money, training, and buying moves.

[*][b] Progression and Customization [/b]  
The ability to purchase new techniques and train up your stats adds a satisfying layer of depth and personal growth.

[*][b] Budget Pricing [/b]  
It’s very cheap, making it an easy impulse buy for those curious about quirky indie fighters.
[/list]  

[h2] BAD [/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b] Stiff, Unrefined Controls [/b]  
Fighting feels clunky and sometimes unresponsive, which can drag down the overall experience.

[*][b] Buggy Execution [/b]  
Bugs and technical issues crop up, typical of Crain Soft’s smaller projects, and can occasionally interrupt progress.

[*][b] Forgettable Story [/b]  
The narrative is barebones—just another “earn money to open a dojo” plot with little emotional investment.
[/list]  

[h2] Final Thought [/h2]  
Karate Master 2: Knock Down Blow is a strange, budget-friendly blend of sim and fighting game. The control issues and simple story won’t appeal to everyone, but if you’re looking for something different and don’t mind a few rough edges, it’s worth picking up in a sale or bundle.

Took me about 6 hours to beat, can probably be beaten quicker. There's two achievements for beating opponents I never encountered in the game, so probably some hidden stuff I didn't find. Only ran into one bug - a random match wouldn't end after a knock out so I had to close the game. Didn't happen again. 

I played with keyboard and mouse. My forearms and fingers felt the burn in some of the training minigames with how much I was pressing "a" "d" "j" "k" "u" "i" but it's an easy control scheme and felt good to use - which kind of surprised me because on paper it sounds terrible imo lmao. There were two moves I couldn't replicate with keyboard and mouse I had to plug in controller for because the inputs wouldn't register all at once. There's a section where in order to learn a move, you have to do it ten times, and in order to unlock a tournament you have to know every move so. Other than those two moves, played fine with keyboard (and never used those moves again other than learning them lmao).

The main appeal of the game is the music and gameplay. The action is surprisingly fun, and the music is good stuff perfect for some intense combat, I vibe with the menu musics too. The story is simple and straight forward, not much there. Just your typical old karate movie as a game. Not sure if the dialogue itself is rough, or if its specifically the English translation, buy boy howdy is some of the dialogue a little out there. But in a good, charming way I could appreciate as throwback to over the top karate movies.

The only actual downside about the game I'd say is the bone-break mechanic, which seems like any opponent has a random chance to break your bone and end the fight immediately regardless of the health of the limb (green, yellow, orange, red). In the final tournament, I'm not sure if it was super bad RNG or the tournament is actually turned up, but my dudes bones kept getting dusted despite having full health. The amount of random one shot defeats in the final tournament made me repeat it a few times and was kind of annoying lmao. Other than that? No complaints.
